title: A yokozuna split across two parallel worlds, and walking straight into walls turned out to be the whole game
author: office-canard
selftext:
SUMOVERSE is a one-screen puzzle. A yokozuna has been split into two parallel worlds, and every move you make happens in both at once. Press a direction and both halves step the same way.



\- Hit a wall and that half shoves it and stays put, while the other half keeps moving. That's how you pull them out of step.

\- The floor you step off falls away behind you.

\- Every shove costs one strength.

\- Grab the yakitori in each world, then bring both halves onto the ring at the very same moment.



It started as a mirror puzzle. Two sides of the glass, different worlds, the same movement. Parallel worlds turned out to be much less confusing to control. At first I pulled the halves apart with one-way paths and moving walkways. Then came walking into a wall without hesitation, and that became the heart of the game.



Why sumo? I wanted a character nobody could read at a glance, something that makes you go "what is this?" That felt right for a game about the multiverse. Why it ended up being sumo, I honestly don't know.



How AI fit in:

Claude wrote all of the code: three.js r128 and plain JS, the rules, the controls, the tools that generate stages, and the checks.



\- The yokozuna is a Mixamo character, repainted. Claude built the mawashi, the rope and the topknot in code and attached them to the skeleton. I picked the animations.

\- Everything else (yakitori, ring, boxes, floors, teleporters, both worlds) is geometry built in code. No image AI.

\- Music is four tracks by Monume on Pixabay. Some sound effects come from free sound sites, and the rest Claude synthesized with Web Audio.

\- The 200 stages are generated. Stages 1 to 50 were grown one by one to a target move count, climbing from 6 moves to 30. Stages 51 to 200 use every gadget on a 7x7 board, with shortest solutions of 28 to 30 moves. A script checks every stage: the hint solves it in the shortest number of moves, and it can't be solved with only one strength.



What playing it caught:

\- One early stage took 66 moves, and only 2 of them were wall shoves. The other 60 were both halves just walking together. So difficulty is now measured by the moves that pull the halves apart, not by total moves.

\- Most dead ends came from pointless wall shoves. I said "think in tiles, not roads," we rebuilt the boards one tile at a time, and dead-end moves dropped by about half.

\- I found teleporters that put you right back where you started. 26 stages were rebuilt.



Free to play in your browser:

[https://office-canard.itch.io/sumoverse](https://office-canard.itch.io/sumoverse)

comments.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
comments.body: I tried the first two tutorials: the second showed the strength cost immediately when one half hit a wall and the other moved on. For the generated stages, it would be interesting to watch where a few playtesters undo or restart alongside your separation-move count. Two boards can need the same number of shoves but have very different numbers of tempting dead ends.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: Exactly. I built this with just me and an AI, doing everything we could to make the puzzles interesting, but there's every chance someone will pick a move I never saw coming. I'd love to get it in front of a lot of people and hear what they think.

replies.author: ArtificialBeingsInc
replies.body: r/playmygame could be another place to ask for feedback if you haven’t shared it there this month. They ask for a free playable build, a direct link, a short description and your role; there’s a post template in the sidebar. You could ask players, ‘What was the first move you undid, and what did you expect to happen?’ That might surface the surprising choices you’re looking for.

replies.author: office-canard
replies.body: Thanks, I hadn't thought of r/playmygame. I like that question a lot too. I'll give it a try.
